read.sections.0.text.source: AI tools that write, answer questions or translate learn from training data. For them, it is a huge amount of writing, much of it from the internet. People speak thousands of languages, but most big AI tools learned mainly from English. A low-resource language has little digital material that computers can use for a task. This might be writing, recordings or word lists. The name is about data, not about the language or its speakers. About 200 million people speak Swahili, but there is not enough Swahili writing online for AI to learn well. In Harbourside, Language C is like this.
read.sections.0.text.back: AI tools that write, answer questions or translate learn from training data. For these tools, training data is a very large amount of writing, mostly from the internet. People speak thousands of languages, but most big AI tools learned mainly from English. A low-resource language is a language that has little digital material a computer can use for a task. This material might be writing, recordings or word lists. The name is about data, not about the language or its speakers. About 200 million people speak Swahili, but there is not enough Swahili writing online for AI to learn well. In Harbourside, Language C is like this.
read.sections.0.text.note: "Low-resource language" is "bahasa kurang sumber" (a language lacking resources). Malaysian NLP papers also say "bahasa sumber rendah"; a reviewer should pick one. The text says straight after that the name is about data, not the language or its speakers, so keep that sentence whatever term is chosen.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Tools that write, answer or translate learn from training data. This is lots of writing from the web. Most big AI tools learned from English. Some languages have little writing or speech for computers. We call this a low-resource language. The name is about data. It is not about the language or the people. About 200 million people speak Swahili. But there is not much written in it online.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Tools that write, answer or translate learn from training data. This data is a lot of writing from the web. Most big AI tools learned from English. read.sections.1.heading.source: Who gets left out, and why
read.sections.1.heading.back: Who gets left behind, and why

read.sections.1.text.source: When a tool works badly in a language, its speakers get worse help. How much writing a language has online is linked to history and power. In Harbourside, schools and offices mostly use Languages A and B. So little is written in Language C. Masakhane is a group of African researchers. It says African languages have a small place in tech partly because of colonialism. That was when other countries ruled much of Africa. The people who build AI tools also choose which languages to include.
read.sections.1.text.back: When a tool works badly in a language, its speakers get worse help. How much writing a language has online is linked to history and power. In Harbourside, schools and offices mostly use Languages A and B. So only a little is written in Language C. Masakhane is a group of African researchers. The group says African languages have a small place in technology partly because of colonialism. That was the time when other countries ruled much of Africa. The people who build AI tools also choose which languages to include.
read.sections.1.text.note: "Colonialism" is "penjajahan", the word Malaysian history books use. The sensitive note asks teachers to keep this short.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: A tool can work badly in a language. Then its speakers get worse help. This is linked to history and power. In Harbourside, schools use Languages A and B. Some African experts say the past matters too. Other countries once ruled much of Africa. That is one reason their languages are left out. AI builders choose which languages to use.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: A tool can work badly in a language. So its speakers get worse help. This is linked to history and power. In Harbourside, schools use Languages A and B. read.sections.2.heading.source: People build tools for their own languages
read.sections.2.heading.back: People build tools for their own languages

read.sections.2.text.source: Now many people are building tools for their own languages. In Singapore, a programme paid for by the government, AI Singapore, builds models called SEA-LION. A 2025 paper by its team says they support 11 languages used in the region, including Burmese, Khmer, Tamil and Vietnamese. But learning from a language is not the same as working well in it. The team's main tests covered only four of those languages. In Jakarta in November 2024, two companies launched Sahabat-AI for Bahasa Indonesia, Javanese and Sundanese. Its makers said it beat similar models, but was at an early stage. Masakhane's name means “We build together” in isiZulu. Its members build tools for African languages, with the people who speak them. Speakers can help a tool fit their community, but people still need to test it.
read.sections.2.text.back: Now many people are building tools for their own languages. In Singapore, a government-funded programme, AI Singapore, builds models called SEA-LION. A 2025 paper by its team states that the models support 11 languages used in this region, including Burmese, Khmer, Tamil and Vietnamese. But learning from a language is not the same as working well in that language. The team's main tests covered only four of those languages. In Jakarta in November 2024, two companies launched Sahabat-AI for Indonesian, Javanese and Sundanese. Its makers said it beat similar models, but was still at an early stage. The name Masakhane means “Let us build together” in isiZulu. Its members build tools for African languages, together with the people who speak them. Speakers can help a tool suit their community, but people still need to test it.
read.sections.2.text.note: Language names follow Malaysian usage: bahasa Myanmar (Burmese), Khmer, Tamil, Vietnam, Jawa, Sunda. "Bahasa Indonesia" in the English is "bahasa Indonesia". Masakhane's meaning is given in Malay, "Kita bina bersama" (inclusive "we"), not in isiZulu.

It makes tools for African languages. Speakers can help a tool fit their community. But people must still test it.

watch.summary.source: This video asks why AI tools work better in some languages than in others. A tool like a chatbot learns by reading lots of writing. The video says it is like a giant bookshop. But the bookshop has a problem. Most of its books are in English and a few other big languages. Languages with little writing online are called low-resource languages. The tools know much less about them. The video looks at two of these, Jamaican Patois and Catalan. It also shows researchers who built an open model in many languages, with help from local communities. The presenter says a few big companies decide what goes into these tools. He says it matters to everyone that AI tools include many languages.

Languages with little writing online are called low-resource languages. AI tools know far less about these languages. The video looks at two of them, that is, Jamaican Patois and Catalan. It also shows researchers who built an open model in many languages, with help from local communities. The presenter says a few big companies decide what goes into these tools. He says it matters to everyone that AI tools include many languages.

educatorNotes.0.source: The Harbourside results (19, 15 and 6 of 20) are made up. The real facts, with their scope: Stanford HAI (2025) defines low-resource languages as those with limited computer-readable data, and gives Swahili (about 200 million speakers) as an example; “low-resource” is about the data for a task (writing, recordings, labelled examples), never about a language's worth or its speakers' skill, and a language can be low-resource for one task and not another. SEA-LION: the 2025 paper (arXiv 2504.05747, version 4, October 2025) describes Llama-SEA-LION-8B-IT and Gemma-SEA-LION-9B-IT, built by AI Singapore with NUS and funded by Singapore's National Research Foundation; the family supports 11 languages (English, Chinese, Indonesian, Vietnamese, Malay, Thai, Burmese, Lao, Filipino, Tamil and Khmer). Supporting a language in training is not proof that it works well: the paper's main benchmark (SEA-HELM) tested only Indonesian, Vietnamese, Thai and Tamil, and a wider test (SEACrowd) covered 31 regional languages but only classic language tasks, not chat; the authors list this as a limitation. The first SEA-LION model (Context, February 2024) was trained on text that was about 63% English, and critics warned that regional models can repeat the views of powerful groups. Sahabat-AI: GoTo's press release (15 November 2024) says it was co-developed with Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison, launched with 8- and 9-billion-parameter models for Bahasa Indonesia, Javanese and Sundanese (Batak and Balinese planned), is open source, and “demonstrated leading performance” against similar open models; that is the makers' claim, with no published scores in the release, and it calls the project early. Masakhane's own description links the small place of African languages in technology partly to colonialism. Older learners could discuss who owns these tools and who tests them.

SEA-LION: the 2025 paper (arXiv 2504.05747, version 4, October 2025) describes Llama-SEA-LION-8B-IT and Gemma-SEA-LION-9B-IT, built by AI Singapore with NUS and funded by Singapore's National Research Foundation; this family of models supports 11 languages (English, Chinese, Indonesian, Vietnamese, Malay, Thai, Burmese, Lao, Filipino, Tamil and Khmer). Supporting a language in training is not proof that it works well: the paper's main benchmark (SEA-HELM) tested only Indonesian, Vietnamese, Thai and Tamil, and a wider test (SEACrowd) covered 31 regional languages but only classic language tasks, not chat; its authors list this as a limitation. The first SEA-LION model (Context, February 2024) was trained on text that was about 63% English, and critics warned that regional models can repeat the views of powerful groups. Sahabat-AI: GoTo's press statement (15 November 2024) states that it was co-developed with Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison, launched with 8- and 9-billion-parameter models for Indonesian, Javanese and Sundanese (Batak and Balinese planned), is open source, and “demonstrated leading performance” (showed leading performance) against similar open models; that is its makers' claim, with no published scores in the statement, and it calls the project still at an early stage. Masakhane's own description links the small place of African languages in technology partly to colonialism. Older learners can discuss who owns these tools and who tests them.
